one_liner: RocksDB plugin that stores large values in separate blob files (WiscKey-style) to cut write amplification versus plain RocksDB.
what_it_does: Titan wraps RocksDB as a StackableDB (rocksdb::titandb::TitanDB) and moves values of at least min_blob_size (default 4 KB) out of the LSM tree into append-only blob files, leaving a small blob index in the SST. The API is the RocksDB API with TitanOptions/TitanCFOptions, so Put/Get/Delete/iterators/column families work unchanged, but Merge, SingleDelete and DisableFileDeletions return NotSupported. It is the value-separation engine inside TiKV.
how_it_is_fast: Key-value separation from the WiscKey paper: compaction rewrites only keys and small blob indexes, not the large values, so write amplification and compaction I/O drop sharply for big values. Separation happens in TitanTableBuilder during flush/compaction, so the foreground write path stays RocksDB's. Blob-file garbage collection is driven by table-property collectors and flush/compaction listeners that track a per-file discardable ratio (default 0.5); optional Level Merge rewrites blobs during compaction of the last two levels to keep them sorted. Smaller SSTs also leave more block cache for index/filter/data blocks, which helps point reads.
when_to_use: Write- or update-heavy workloads with values of roughly 1 KB and up (PingCAP reports the gain grows with value size; 16 KB values benefit most).
RocksDB deployments limited by compaction I/O, write stalls or SSD wear from write amplification.
Point-lookup-dominated reads on large values where the base LSM tree shrinking to keys plus indexes lets more of it fit in block cache.
Mixed value sizes: values below min_blob_size stay inline in RocksDB, so only the large ones pay the blob indirection.
You already build against TiKV's RocksDB fork (tikv/rocksdb 8.10.tikv) or run TiKV.
when_not_to_use: Range-scan-heavy workloads: PingCAP says Titan underperforms RocksDB on range queries, and TiDB docs put the drop at 40% to a few times slower; each scanned value is an extra blob-file read.

Disk-space-constrained deployments: space amplification is higher than RocksDB (TiDB docs: can reach about twice RocksDB before GC catches up), and per-record blob compression compresses worse than RocksDB's per-block compression.
Small values (well under 1 KB): they stay inline, so you pay plugin complexity for no gain.
Workloads that need Merge operators or SingleDelete, which Titan rejects with NotSupported.
Projects pinned to upstream facebook/rocksdb: master uses the TiKV-fork-only kTypeTitanBlobIndex value type, so it does not build against or interoperate with upstream RocksDB.

integration.dependencies: RocksDB source tree (CMake clones tikv/rocksdb branch 8.10.tikv by default); optional snappy/lz4/zstd/zlib/bzip2, jemalloc; gflags for tools
integration.platforms: not documented; build files handle x86-64 (SSE4.2), aarch64 and ppc64le like RocksDB, CI and production use is Linux (TiKV)
integration.thread_safety: Same model as RocksDB DB (concurrent reads/writes on one handle); repo carries a thread_safety_test
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same rocksdb::DB interface via StackableDB, but needs TiKV's RocksDB fork, rejects Merge/SingleDelete, and an on-disk Titan DB cannot simply be reopened by plain RocksDB (use blob_run_mode kFallback to rewrite values back into SSTs first)

gotchas: Blob files are not reclaimed until GC runs; space depends on blob_file_discardable_ratio and GC thread count (max_background_gc default 1).
MultiGet is a loop over single Gets and each Get without a snapshot takes a ManagedSnapshot; point reads also take several extra mutexes versus RocksDB (issue #139).
blob_run_mode kFallback / kReadOnly exist to migrate away; there is no direct rollback to plain RocksDB.
Open issues report crashes on missing blob files under races (#328, #186); check TiKV release notes before relying on a given branch.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Titan over TerarkDB when values are large (>= 1 KB) and the bottleneck is write/compaction amplification rather than read QPS or compression ratio, and when you want a maintained plugin that tracks a recent RocksDB (8.10 fork) rather than a fork frozen near RocksDB 6.x.
verified_claims_summary: PingCAP's April 2019 blog ran go-ycsb against TiKV on Titan versus TiKV on RocksDB (64 GB dataset, TiKV capped at 32 GB RAM, 1 KB and 16 KB values) on a 40-core Xeon E5-2630 v4 with 128 GB RAM and a SATA SSD, reporting about 70% higher load throughput and 180% higher update throughput, better point gets, worse range scans and slightly higher space use; compiler, flags and exact versions are not given and the numbers include TiKV's Raft log overhead.
status_note: Maintained by the TiKV team at a slow cadence (last master commit 2026-04-29), Apache-2.0, and in production as TiKV's default engine for new clusters since v7.6.0, but usable outside TiKV only if you adopt TiKV's RocksDB fork.
